newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Subversion trials worry Indonesian rights body.
newsitem.headline: Subversion trials worry Indonesian rights body.

text.p: A leading member of Indonesia's official National Commission on Human Rights said on Wednesday the body was concerned about the lack of clear reasons for the imminent prosecution of 10 activists for subversion.

Commission deputy chairman Marzuki Darusman said after meeting a number of the accused in prison on Tuesday that despite being arrested soon after Jakarta's July 27 riots, it was still not clear why they were being tried in six separate cases later this month.

"One question still lingers. Why were they detained? What is the connection between their detention and the events of July 27," Darusman told Reuters on the sidelines of a human rights conference in Jakarta.

"The connection has not clearly been established and (the accused) seem to have the strong impression that the questions (during interrogation) were not directed at their involvement in the July 27 riots but connected with something else," he said.

The dossiers of nine activists from the People's Democratic Party (PRD) and independent labour leader Muchtar Pakpahan were submitted to two Jakarta courts on Monday with officials saying they expected the trials to begin within two weeks.
Subversion carries the death penalty in Indonesia.

The government and military blamed the small left-wing PRD for being behind the riots, regarded as being the worst in more than 20 years, in a barrage of comments in the wake of the disturbances in which at least five people died.

In October, the commission reported that the riots started after police backed an attack by rivals of ousted Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) leader Megawati Sukarnoputri on her supporters occupying the party's headquarters.
Last month, a Jakarta court found 115 Megawati supporters guilty of disobeying police orders to disperse while defending the building but dismissed charges of assault against them.
After imposing a four-month three-day sentence, they were all released with time served.
Darusman said the Attorney-General's department had told the commission the government had a strong basis on which to bring the subversion charges which would stand up in court.

"I think it is not easy to understand why these cases are being tried. It is something that we have not been able to establish. Perhaps there are things that the government knows that we don't know yet which will come up in the trials," he said.

Lawyers for the PRD members told the commission last month their clients had been questioned about events up to three years old and said some had been tortured while briefly in the custody of military intelligence soon after their arrest in August.
Darusman said the commission members had found the suspects, including PRD leader Budiman Sudjatmiko, in good health.
"We interviewed Budiman and he said they were not actually physically abused but the whole process of interogation was quite wearisome and was very tiring," Darusman said.
